FrMS88-de3150-d1e111.summary: Poses the seventh question: whether the notion of being is prescinded from the other formal notions in God. Against: Hilary says diversity is not to be admitted in God, and prescission is diversity. For: Dionysius says there is some otherness and diversity in God. Meyronnes sets out to exclude two views of two doctors (Joannes and Petrus): one holds that being has one concept but not one notion, unprescinded from others; the other that it has one unprescinded formal notion, not said in quid of all.
claims: Hilary seems to exclude diversity, and so prescission, in God.
Reported views: being has one unprescinded concept, or one unprescinded notion.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e137.summary: Against the first doctor, raises four contradictions, the first: the same concept would be common and not common, proper and not proper, since the certain concept of being is common while the concept of each doubtful item is not, and a concept both certain and doubtful of two would be both common and not common to them.
claims: An unprescinded concept of being would be both common and proper.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e157.summary: Second contradiction: the same concept would be repugnant and not repugnant, since the concept of being is compossible with all, while concepts like 'man' are not.
claims: An unprescinded concept of being would be both repugnant and non-repugnant to others.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e170.summary: Third contradiction: the same concept would be transcendental and not transcendental, being transcendental as being but not as man.
claims: An unprescinded concept of being would be both transcendental and not.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e178.summary: Fourth contradiction: the same concept would be abstract and not abstract, since the concept of being is abstract while those of its inferiors are not.
claims: An unprescinded concept of being would be both abstract and not.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e185.summary: States the possible reply that the unity of being is a unity of indetermination.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e192.summary: Rejects that reply by the same reasoning (the concept of being would be one by indetermination and the others not), and because the ten categories have determinate concepts while being has an indeterminate one, which cannot be said of the same. Concludes that if the doctors are taken as they sound, the same contradictions apply to both, though he believes they did not mean this. Then argues that the notion of being is prescinded from all others: by the first complex principle, when something belongs to one formal notion of itself and not to another, they are distinct; to beatify belongs to God as God but not to being as being, else it would belong to every being.
claims: Indeterminate and determinate cannot be said of the same concept.
The notion of being is prescinded from all other notions.
To beatify belongs to God as God but not to being as being, so deity and entity are distinct notions.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e238.summary: Answers the reply that this holds only of being in general: he speaks of the notion of being found in all things and proves that it is distinguished from deity.
claims: The notion of being found in all things is distinct from deity.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e245.summary: Second argument: when something is really repugnant to a thing by one formal notion and not by another, those notions are somehow distinct; finitude is repugnant to God by deity but not by entity, else to every being.
claims: Finitude is repugnant to God by reason of deity, not of entity.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e258.summary: Third argument: the same intellect cannot be certain and doubtful of the same formal notion; we are certain of divine entity but doubt the proper notion of deity.
claims: Certainty about divine entity and doubt about deity show their notions are distinct.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e268.summary: Fourth argument: the same notion cannot be naturally knowable and not; the notion of deity is not naturally knowable, while that of entity is.
claims: Entity is naturally knowable, deity is not.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e277.summary: Raises four counterarguments, the first: when one notion is the other, neither is prescinded or distinct; the notions of entity and deity are such that one is the other.
claims: Objection: deity is entity, so they are not prescinded.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e286.summary: Second counterargument: the divine essence in its precision is something positive or not; if not, nothing; if so, a being.
claims: Objection: the divine essence in its precision must be a being.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e293.summary: Third counterargument: the formal notion of deity is something or nothing; not nothing, therefore a being.
claims: Objection: the notion of deity is something, hence a being.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e298.summary: Fourth counterargument: a notion that is every notion with nothing added to it is not prescinded; the notion of being is such, since anything added would be either being (being added to being) or nothing.
claims: Objection: nothing can be added to being, so being is every notion.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e309.summary: Reply to the first: although one notion is the other absolutely and in some way, it is not so in every way; the notion of deity is not in every way the same as that of entity.
claims: Deity and entity are the same in some way but not in every way.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e321.summary: Answers the demand that non-identity be referred to extremes by distinguishing two abstractions: one by first-intention names, where one is always said of the other; one by second-intention names, where this is not always true (e.g. 'the defined is the definition' is false as second intention, though 'man is rational animal' is true as first). The definition of being is not the definition of deity; 'deity is entity' is true at the first abstraction, but 'deity is formally entity' is false, since 'formally' signals the second abstraction.
claims: First-intention abstraction allows deity to be called entity; second-intention abstraction ('formally') does not.
Deity is entity but not formally entity.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e347.summary: Reply to the second: as a difference prescinded from its genus is the genus denominatively but not quidditatively, so the divine essence prescinded from entity is entity denominatively; it is not quidditatively the positive that is formally entity.
claims: The divine essence prescinded from entity is entity denominatively, not quidditatively.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e358.summary: Reply to the third: deity is something by its own 'aliquity', but it does not follow that it is formally entity.
claims: Deity is something by its own aliquity without being formally entity.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e365.summary: Objection: where a definition is predicated the predication seems formal, and the definition of being is predicated of deity.
claims: Objection: predicating the definition of being of deity would be formal predication.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e370.summary: Reply: a definition is predicated only in the way the definitum is defined; being is defined only through a second intention, so that intention is said of God as it is said of being — denominatively, not quidditatively.
claims: Being is defined only by a second intention, which is said of God denominatively.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e386.summary: Adds that if asked what this formal notion is, it can be called a second intention, as the formal notion of entity is taken here; but when a formal notion is a second intention it supposits for a first intention.
claims: The formal notion of entity, as here taken, is a second intention suppositing for a first.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e396.summary: Reply to the fourth: 'every notion with nothing added' can mean quidditatively or only identically and denominatively; in the first sense the major is true and the minor false, in the second the major is false. Being is every notion denominatively, not quidditatively, as 'rational' is animal denominatively but adds to animal quidditatively. Then argues to his conclusion: a concept not in every way the same as all others with nothing added is prescinded from them, and being is such.
claims: Being is every notion denominatively but not quidditatively.
The concept of being is prescinded from all others.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e440.summary: First proof: a concept identical with others with nothing added is merely equivocal, since the equivocal adds nothing to its equivocates but the name; on the opponent's view the concept of being adds only a name to the items of which it is said.
claims: A concept identical with its inferiors without addition would be merely equivocal.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e451.summary: Second and third proofs: a concept that is every non-transcendental concept with nothing added is not transcendental, and on the opponent's view being is the concept of the ten categories with nothing added; and a concept which is a singular concept with nothing added is not universal.
claims: Such a concept of being would be neither transcendental nor universal.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e462.summary: Fourth proof: a concept that is all others indifferently has no greater unity than they; singular concepts have only unity of aggregation or order, so being would have only that, which is manifestly false.
claims: The concept of being has more than an aggregative unity.
concepts: unity of the concept of being

FrMS88-de3150-d1e475.summary: Notes that this view reduces to that of older doctors, that the intellect is certain of one of two indeterminately and doubtful of either determinately.
claims: Reported view: certainty concerns an indeterminate disjunct.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e482.summary: Argues against it: the intellect is certain either of neither, or of one, or of both together, or of one indistinctly and indeterminately.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e492.summary: If of neither, the conclusion follows, since a concept neutral to two determinates is prescinded from them. Not of one, since God is not finite, and his infinity is doubted; not of both, since no one is certain of the falsehood that God is finite and infinite.
claims: A concept neutral to two determinates is prescinded from them.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e505.summary: If of one indeterminately, the earlier argument applies: we would then be as certain that God is triune, incarnate, or dead as that he is a being, since we are equally certain he is triune or not as first or not.
claims: Indeterminate certainty would extend absurdly to the Trinity and Incarnation.

FrMS88-de3150-d1e521.summary: Reply to Hilary's opening argument: he speaks of diversity in nature.
claims: Hilary denies diversity of nature in God, not formal prescission.

FrMS88-de3150.summary: The seventh question of the prologue asks whether the notion of being is 'precise' (prescinded, distinct) from the other formal notions in God. Meyronnes sets aside the positions of two doctors (identified as Joannes and Petrus), one holding that being has one concept but not one notion and that this concept is not prescinded from others, the other that it has one formal notion not prescinded and not said in quid of all. Taken as they sound, both views attribute contradictory features (common and proper, compossible and repugnant, transcendental and not, abstract and not, indeterminate and determinate) to one concept. Meyronnes argues that the notion of being is prescinded from all others, including deity, because something belongs to God as God (to beatify) and not to being as being, finitude is repugnant to God by deity but not by entity, we are certain of divine entity while doubtful of the proper notion of deity, and deity, unlike entity, is not naturally knowable. He answers objections by holding that deity and entity are the same in some way but not in every way; that deity is entity in first-intention abstraction but not 'formally', a second-intention claim; that the divine essence is entity denominatively, not quidditatively; and that being is every notion denominatively but not quidditatively. He concludes that a concept which is all others with nothing added would be equivocal, not transcendental, singular, and only an aggregate unity — and that the old doctrine of certainty about an indeterminate disjunct fails, since it would make us as certain of the Trinity and Incarnation as of God's being. Hilary's denial of diversity in God concerns diversity in nature.
claims: The formal notion of being is prescinded from the other formal notions in God, including deity.
Deity and entity are the same in some way but not in every way; deity is not formally entity.
The divine essence, prescinded from entity, is entity denominatively and not quidditatively.
A concept that is identical with all others without addition would be equivocal, non-transcendental, singular, and merely aggregative.
Certainty about an indeterminate disjunction cannot explain certainty that God is a being.
